extracted.intended_audience: communications and public relations professionals, measurement & evaluation practitioners, agencies, in-house communicators, government communicators, NGOs, and charities
extracted.subtask_description: High-level industry principles for planning, measuring, and evaluating communications activity; intended to guide PR/communications practitioners across commercial, public-sector, and non-profit organisations in defining goals, selecting measures, and interpreting impact with integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting goals is an absolute prerequisite to communications planning, measurement, and evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.description: The founding principle of SMART (specific, measurable, actionable, relevant, and time-bound) goals as a foundation for communications planning has been promoted to an essential prerequisite. It pushes measurement and evaluation as a core component of the planning process, articulating target outcomes and how progress towards these will be assessed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goals must be set before planning and measurement; use SMART criteria; clearly articulate target outcomes and the means by which progress will be assessed. Measurement and evaluation should be embedded in planning rather than an afterthought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement and evaluation should identify outputs, outcomes, and potential impact.
rubrics_metrics.description: Previously, the Principles recommended measuring outcomes, rather than simply counting outputs. The updated principles extend this to consider longer term impact of communications strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and differentiate short-term outputs (e.g., content produced, impressions), outcomes (changes in awareness, attitudes, behaviour) and longer-term impact (societal or organisational change). Think about the channels being impacted and the change desired through campaigns, events and activations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcomes and impact should be identified for stakeholders, society, and the organization.
rubrics_metrics.description: From the original focus on business metrics, such as sales and revenue, the 2020 update embraces a more holistic view of performance. It allows the model to be more inclusive of a broader range of organisations and communications roles that are not necessarily profit-driven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defining outcomes/impact, consider multiple beneficiaries and perspectives — stakeholders (e.g., customers, partners), society (public interest, social outcomes), and the organisation — rather than solely business/financial metrics. Adapt measures to non-commercial objectives where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication measurement and evaluation should include both qualitative and quantitative analysis.
rubrics_metrics.description: “To understand the full impact of your work, it is crucial that you use the full suite of methods to measure those outcomes,” summarised Levine in describing the evolution of this principle to not just quantify but also understand how messages are being received, believed and interpreted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a mixed-methods approach: quantitative metrics (reach, impressions, conversions) combined with qualitative methods (message testing, sentiment analysis, interviews, focus groups) to understand interpretation, belief, and meaning. Avoid relying solely on counts or metrics without contextual qualitative insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: AVEs are not the value of communication.
rubrics_metrics.description: The message remains consistent and clear; “we continue to believe that AVEs do not demonstrate the value of our work.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using Advertising Value Equivalents (AVEs) as a proxy for communications value. Employ richer, multi-faceted approaches to assess value and impact rather than simplistic monetary equivalencies of media space/time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holistic communication measurement and evaluation includes all relevant online and offline channels.
rubrics_metrics.description: Our founding principle that social media can and should be measured is so obvious today. The 2020 iteration reflects the game-changing shift in social communications’ capabilities, opportunities, and influence, such that all relevant online and offline channels should be measured and evaluated equally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure and evaluate across earned, owned, shared, and paid channels for consistency towards common goals. Treat online and offline channels comprehensively rather than privileging one over the other; ensure cross-channel clarity in methodology and reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication measurement and evaluation are rooted in integrity and transparency to drive learning and insights.
rubrics_metrics.description: Sound, consistent, and sustained measurement calls for integrity and transparency in recognition of today’s attention to data privacy and stewardship as organisations comply with new regulations, such as GDPR. This is also a statement that measurement isn’t simply about data collection and tracking, but about learning from evaluation and applying insight back into communications planning. It recognises the need to be transparent about the context in which programmes are run and being aware of any bias that may exist in the tools, methodologies and interpretations applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure ethical data stewardship, compliance with privacy regulations (e.g., GDPR), and transparent reporting of methods, context, and limitations. Use evaluation to drive learning and improvement, and disclose potential biases in tools, methodologies, and interpretations.
